note: Rome: kingdom, republic, empire — and after 395 the Eastern Roman Empire ruled from Constantinople.
The western half of the empire after the division of 395, until the deposition of Romulus Augustulus (476) and the death of Julius Nepos (480).
Croesus's kingdom, ruled from Sardis, until Cyrus conquered it in 547 BC.
The empire of Nebuchadnezzar and Nabonidus, until Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC.
Native pharaohs: before the Persian conquest of 525 BC, and again from 404 to 343 BC.
The empire of Cyrus, Darius and Xerxes, until Alexander's conquest (334–330 BC).
Independent Greek poleis and leagues — Athens, Sparta, Corinth, Syracuse, Massalia, Rhodes, the Achaean and Aetolian leagues and many more.
The Phoenician city of Carthage and its empire in Africa, Sicily, Sardinia and Spain, until 146 BC.
A league of independent Etruscan city-states.
Philip II's Macedon, Alexander's empire, the warring successors, and then the Antigonid kingdom until Rome's victory at Pydna (168 BC).
The largest successor kingdom, from Syria to Iran, shrinking until Pompey ended it in 64 BC.
The Macedonian pharaohs from Ptolemy I to Cleopatra VII, ruling from Alexandria.
The Attalid kingdom, enlarged by Rome in 188 BC and bequeathed to Rome in 133 BC.
Hellenistic kingdom on the Sea of Marmara, bequeathed to Rome in 74 BC.
Mithridatic kingdom on the Black Sea; under Mithridates VI it fought Rome for 25 years.
Celtic tribes settled in central Anatolia in the 270s BC; a kingdom under Deiotarus and Amyntas, a Roman province from 25 BC.
The Ariarathid and later Archelaid kings, Roman clients, until annexation in AD 17.
Orontid, Artaxiad and Arsacid kings; briefly a great power under Tigranes the Great (95–55 BC); contested by Rome and Persia.
The Arsacid kings, ruling from Ctesiphon over Mesopotamia and Iran.
The Persian dynasty that overthrew the Parthians in 224, Rome's great rival for four centuries.
Berber kingdom of Masinissa and Jugurtha, annexed by Caesar in 46 BC.
Berber kingdom of the Mauri — later ruled by Juba II for Augustus — annexed in AD 40.
Saharan kingdom of the Fezzan oases.
The Nubian kingdom of Napata and Meroë.
Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia, successors of Kush; Christian from the 540s.
Red Sea trading kingdom in Ethiopia; Christian from c. 340.
The Arab kingdom of Petra, rich from the incense trade, annexed by Trajan in 106.
The Jewish kingdom of the Hasmoneans, then of Herod and his sons.
Small Hellenistic-Iranian kingdom on the upper Euphrates.
Aramaean kingdom of the Abgar dynasty, a buffer between Rome and Parthia.
Odaenathus and Queen Zenobia of Palmyra took over Rome's East; Aurelian destroyed their empire in 272.
Breakaway Roman state of Postumus and his successors in Gaul, Britain and (until 269) Spain, reunited by Aurelian in 274.
The Thracian kingdom of the Odrysians, later a Roman client, annexed in AD 46.
The Dacian kingdom of Burebista and Decebalus, conquered by Trajan in 106.
Greek-Sarmatian kingdom on the Kerch strait, a grain exporter and later a Roman client.
Tervingi and Greuthungi north of the Danube and the Black Sea, until the Huns arrived (376).
The Huns of Uldin, Rua and Attila, dominant from the steppe to the Danube until Attila died (453).
Germanic kingdom on the Tisza and in Transylvania, destroyed by Lombards and Avars in 567.
Theoderic's Goths: in Pannonia, then rulers of Italy (493–553).
Settled in Aquitaine in 418, rulers of most of Spain by 500, with their capital at Toulouse and later Toledo.
Vandals and Alans: in Spain, then rulers of Africa from Carthage (439–533).
Germanic kingdom in Gallaecia, conquered by the Visigoths in 585.
Settled in Savoy in 443, rulers of the Rhône and Saône valleys until the Franks took over (534).
Salian and Rhineland Franks; united by Clovis, who conquered most of Gaul.
Rump Roman state in northern Gaul under Aegidius and Syagrius, conquered by Clovis in 486.
Odoacer, the general who deposed the last western emperor, ruled Italy until Theoderic killed him (493).
Britons who crossed to Armorica, giving it the name Brittany.
Germanic people in Pannonia from the 520s; they invaded Italy in 568.
Steppe nomads who arrived in 558 and took the Carpathian basin in 567–568.
Berber kingdoms of Mauretania and the Aurès, independent of Vandals and Romans.
Arab kingdom of al-Hira, allies of Persia.
Christian Arab federates of Rome guarding the desert frontier.
Christian kingdom of western Georgia, allied to Constantinople.
